content: 1. All individuals should be encouraged to adopt and maintain heart-healthy lifestyle habits, as these are foundational for reducing the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). 2. Statin therapy should be initiated or continued at an intensity appropriate to the individual’s risk profile to effectively lower blood cholesterol levels and reduce ASCVD risk. 3. Adherence to both lifestyle modifications and prescribed drug therapy should be regularly monitored. This includes periodic assessments of lipid levels and evaluations for any safety concerns related to the treatment. 4. For individuals who are unable to tolerate the recommended intensity of statin therapy, the highest intensity of statin that is tolerable should be used to achieve the best possible reduction in ASCVD risk. 5. Clinical ASCVD encompasses conditions such as acute coronary syndromes, a history of myocardial infarction (MI), stable or unstable angina, coronary or other arterial revascularization, stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or peripheral arterial disease presumed to be of atherosclerotic origin. 6. The estimated 10-year risk of ASCVD, often referred to as hard ASCVD risk, includes the first occurrence of nonfatal MI, coronary heart disease (CHD) death, and nonfatal or fatal stroke. This risk is calculated using the Pooled Cohort Equations developed by the Risk Assessment Work Group. 7. Additional factors that may indicate a higher risk of ASCVD include primary LDL-C levels of 160 mg/dL or higher, evidence of genetic hyperlipidemias, a family history of premature ASCVD (onset before age 55 in a first-degree male relative or before age 65 in a first-degree female relative), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels of 2 mg/L or higher, a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score of 300 Agatston units or higher (or at or above the 75th percentile for age, sex, and ethnicity), an ankle-brachial index (ABI) of less than 0.9, or a high lifetime risk of ASCVD. 8. High-risk individuals include those with clinical ASCVD, untreated LDL-C levels of 190 mg/dL or higher (suggesting genetic hypercholesterolemia), or individuals aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes and LDL-C levels between 70 and 189 mg/dL.
